sources.bodyExcerpt: Quick Hit: Foxpedal Defector Fuzz Review — Precision, Clarity, and Dynamic Range in a Compact Analog Circuit | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / practice tips practice tips Quick Hit: Foxpedal Defector Fuzz Review — Precision, Clarity, and Dynamic Range in a Compact Analog Circuit By Liam Carter July 10, 2026 The Foxpedal Defector Fuzz is not another vintage-inspired clone—it’s a precision-engineered, modern analog fuzz pedal designed for dynamic responsiveness, harmonic fidelity, and studio-grade consistency. Measuring 118 mm × 68 mm × 52 mm (4.65″ × 2.68″ × 2.05″) with true-bypass switching and a discrete silicon transistor circuit (2N5088 and 2N5089 matched pair), it delivers 32 dB of gain with Design Philosophy and Circuit Architecture Foxpedal, based in Portland, Oregon, positions the Defector as a ‘fidelity-first’ fuzz. Its core departure from classic designs lies in intentional rejection of passive tone-sucking networks and unregulated bias drift. While most silicon fuzzes (e.g., Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi v1) use cascaded gain stages with RC filtering that attenuates low-end and compresses dynamics, the Defector employs a dual-stage active EQ buffer pre- and post-fuzz core. This architecture isolates the fuzz circuit from pickup impedance variations—a critical factor often overlooked in practice scenarios where players switch between Stratocasters (7.2 kΩ DC resistance) and Les Pauls (14.8 kΩ). Transistor Matching and Thermal Stability Each Defector unit ships with hand-matched 2N5088 (Q1, input stage) and 2N5089 (Q2, output stage) transistors, selected for h FE within ±3% tolerance (measured at V CE = 1V, I C = 1mA). This tight matching reduces inter-stage imbalance and ensures consistent clipping symmetry. Crucially, Foxpedal mounts both transistors on thermally coupled copper pads, achieving No Passive Tone Stack, No Compromise Many pedals insert passive tone controls (e.g., the treble bleed network in the Dunlop Fuzz Face) that load the circuit and degrade high-frequency transient response. The Defector omits such networks entirely. Instead, its single-knob ‘Tone’ control adjusts a fully active Baxandall-style EQ centered at 1.8 kHz, with ±12 dB boost/cut range and Q = 1.4. This preserves signal integrity while offering surgical shaping—essential when practicing legato phrasing or harmonic minor sequences where upper-mid clarity determines intelligibility. Key Controls and Operational Behavior The Defector features three knobs: Volume (output level, calibrated to unity at 12 o’clock), Fuzz (gain staging, logarithmic taper), and Tone (active EQ). All pots are Alpha 9mm sealed units rated for 200,000 cycles. Unlike pedals with ambiguous gain labeling (e.g., “Sustain” on the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff), the Fuzz control delivers linear, repeatable gain increase: from 18 dB at 9 o’clock to 32 dB at 3 o’clock, verified via oscilloscope measurement using a 1 kHz sine wave at −20 dBu input. Volume Control Precision The Volume knob operates with 0.5 dB resolution per 15° rotation near unity—meaning subtle adjustments (e.g., dropping volume by 1.5 dB for cleaner chord comping) are physically precise and audibly distinct. This granularity matters during metronome-based practice: reducing output by exactly 2 dB while maintaining identical pick attack allows focused study of dynamic shading without altering tonal character. Fuzz Knob Linearity and Sweet Spots At 10–2 o’clock, the Fuzz control yields a ‘transparent overdrive’ zone ideal for blues phrasing—retaining string texture and harmonic nuance. Between 2–4 o’clock, it transitions into singing sustain with even-order harmonic emphasis (measured 2nd harmonic at −14.2 dB relative to fundamental). From 4–6 o’clock, odd-order harmonics dominate (3rd at −12.8 dB), delivering articulate distortion suited for jazz-rock fusion lines. The City V2 is a Tube Screamer-style overdrive with extensive voicing options and an independent MOSFET boost. Four knobs (Level, Body, Tone, Drive) shape the core overdrive. A clipping selector toggles between Red LED (aggressive) and MOSFET (smooth) diode options. The Presence switch adds treble clipping, and the Flat switch reduces the mid-forward focus for a more open sound. An independent Ebenezer MOSFET clean boost section runs on its own footswitch. sources.description: The Foxpedal Vixen is an out-of-production overdrive pedal offering versatility and a wide dynamic range. Based on the Foxtail framework, it features 4148 and Nanolog N3 clipping diodes for diverse overdrive tones, from amp-like sparkle boosts to creamy, touch-sensitive gain. sources.snippet: Foxpedal Vixen | AllThePedals
sources.bodyExcerpt: Foxpedal Vixen | AllThePedals Articles Genealogy Browse Search results for " " Gain / Overdrive / Foxpedal Vixen Vixen The Foxpedal Vixen is an out-of-production overdrive pedal offering versatility and a wide dynamic range. Based on the Foxtail framework, it features 4148 and Nanolog N3 clipping diodes for diverse overdrive tones, from amp-like sparkle boosts to creamy, touch-sensitive gain. The Vixen includes Treble, Bass, and Presence controls for precise tonal shaping, suiting various playing styles with its clean boost, fat leads, and medium crunch capabilities. What Foxpedal say about the Vixen Out of Production - all remaining units sold The Vixen is a stunning dimensional overdrive with loads of flexibility and an incredible dynamic range. At its core, The Vixen is based on the framework of our previous pedal, The Foxtail, but is a completely new pedal in almost every way. Featuring a 4148 diode more for more traditional overdrive sounds, The Vixen also features a Nanolog N3 which utilizes “Quantum Tunneling Technology” (yes, you read that correctly) for a completely different experience. This is not just alternate clipping, but is like having two completely different pedals to choose from in one enclosure. Additionally, the tone control features Treble, Bass, and Presence knobs, which has greatly opened its range and made it extremely precise to dial in exactly what you want. At low gain in the N3 mode, with volume at unity and all other settings at noon, The Vixen works very nicely as an “amp-tone sparkle booster.” It enhances your amp to simply become “more” of itself by giving it a slightly beefed up tonal profile by clarifying, but not coloring, your amp's sound. When you increase the gain you’ll find that it is buttery and smooth and extremely touch sensitive to the player’s dynamics. Tonally it turns on a dime, going from a round, “pleasantly-pushed compressor” sound to a crystal clear, clean-amp sound—all entirely based on the player’s interactions. In the 4148 mode, you’re met with more traditional overdrive sounds. That little bit of extra bite and grit to really dig in while still being sparkly. It’s just the right amount of sizzle. It’s perfect for bright, singing leads or big full chords to really fill the space. One thing that is really special is the harmonics of this pedal. It’s almost as if, no matter what you do, you can still clearly hear each individual string. It is extremely articulate. It’s bright without being harsh. It growls without sounding muddy. The Vixen is a truly versatile pedal, well suited for many playing styles. From “Always On” and Preamp functions, to clean boost, to fat creamy leads, to medium crunch it covers a lot of ground. It’s definitely a pedal you need to hear and “feel.” Features: - Level, Presence, Gain, Bass and Treble Knobs - Nanolog N3 clipping - 4148 Diode Clipping - SMT construction - Milled aluminum gold colored knurled knobs - Top Jacks - Soft Footswitch - Standard 9 volt DC/ negative center, NO internal battery option. foxpedal.com What guitarists say... Customers raved about the Foxpedal Vixen, describing it as a versatile pedal that enhances their amp's sound with a warm, crystal-clear boost and tube-like tones. Reviewers highlighted its ability to sing and its suitability for various skill levels, often replacing other popular overdrive pedals, such as the [Tube Screamer], due to its incredible performance. sources.bodyExcerpt: Guitar Pedal X - GPX Blog - Foxpedal's Vixen Dimensional Drive is even more appealing in the flesh and has a Wonderful Depth of Harmonics ao link News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index Enter a search term Search Remember Login Register | Reset Password Xploration • Curation • Recommendation News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index News GPX AI Forums Notifications Popular Highlights 4 of a Kind 12 Degrees of Saturation ArtistArray Best in Class Best of Brands Builder Profiles Colours Expo Guitar Pedal 101 Iconic Gear In Memoriam Pedal Chain Pedal Planet Trifecta Versus Index Enter a search term Search Remember Login Register | Reset Password Filter content by area of interest Amps Boost and Overdrive Delay Distortion Fuzz Guitars Modulation Pitch Reverb Utility All All Foxpedal's Vixen Dimensional Drive is even more appealing in the flesh and has a Wonderful Depth of Harmonics May 25, 2021 19:00 by Stefan Karlsson Boost Boost and Overdrive Foxpedal Harmonic Overdrive Overdrive + - Full Article Read Summary Key Points Foxpedal’s Vixen Dimensional Drive: striking royal-blue/purple finish and two clipping options — Nanalog N3 Quantum Diode and 1N4148. N3 mode: dense, deep harmonic character with reduced top-end; 1N4148: more open, lighter, less low-end and more high frequency. Medium-gain pedal; typical settings: Gain 12–3 o’clock, Presence ~2:30, Volume ~2 o’clock, Bass and Treble often maxed. Not quite as harmonically rich as a Keeley‑Modded Blues Driver, but close and distinct. John and Bruce Snyder took over Foxpedal on Jan 1, 2018; Quiver Tremolo and Novaplex Delay are nearing completion. As of May, the price was £199, sold via the Foxpedal Webstore. May has been a busy month with quite a number of overdrive pedals new on the scene, and within that company the Vixen Dimensional Drive is a particularly special candidate. It has one of the prettiest enclosures you might ever happen upon - with a really special paint-job of a vibrant shade of Royal Blues which is right on the cusp of Purple - so that in certain lights the pedal appears sort of purple - but is most of the time a really deep and vibrant royal blue. I noted before that one of its clipping options is pretty rare - the Nanalog N3 Quantum Diode. And that’s where most of the fun is to be had - with a particularly appealing dense and deep harmonic character with a little less top-end too. It’s not quite as harmonically rich as my Keeley-Modded Blues Driver - but replaces that pedal for this month at least with something pretty close to that sort of richness - while being distinct to itself. The other 1N4148 Diode flavour is a somewhat more open-pored and slightly lighter touch - with less low-end and more high frequency content. John Snyder of Creation Music and Foxpedal fame explained to me why he did not feel it worthwhile to have a second footswitch to toggle those two modes as they are quite distinct. While I largely deploy the same settings on both - and with Bass and Treble Maxed out. This is very much a medium-gain pedal - where I operate the Gain mostly between 12-3 o’c, Presence at around 2:30 o’c, and Volume adjusted to setup - which on mine is around 2 o’c. CC Hybrid2 uses one of each, combining the warm, dark organic tone of germanium with the clarity and sustain of silicon. The Si/Ge transistor pair is selected by ear and biased to deliver a tone with all the best qualities of Germanium and Silicon. CC Hybrid2 is a very stable fuzz that rejects radio transmissions, and the tone does not change with temperature (two common Fuzz Face problems) Hybrid History The original CC Hybrid is named after the Foxrox Captain Coconut (CC) pedal. CC combined a Fuzz Face, Uni-Vibe, and Octavia into one pedal, and it was the first to utilize a Fuzz Face circuit with one silicon and one germanium transistor. Its successor, Captain Coconut2 , was later produced with a plug-in hybrid FuzzCard, in addition to optional all-silicon and all-germanium FuzzCards. The Si/Ge hybrid circuit lived on through the CC Hybrid pedal, produced from 2012-2016. In 2017, it was discontinued and replaced with CC Hybrid2. One foot switch $135.15 $67.58 Quantity : Add to cart SKU: RGS-FR-FESTIVAL Category: Other Description Specifications Reviews Details The Festival Overdrive is a dual-mode overdrive. It features a master volume control and a boost channel with both gain and volume controls. There is a selectable clipping/compression circuit and two tone shaping controls – body and bright. One foot switch bypasses the effect and another foot switch selects between the green and red channels (low gain and high gain). Watch Pete Thorn’s demo above to hear the Festival in action. Body control The Body control on Festival is identical to Voice #1 on the Foxrox ZIM pedal. To help explain this control, heres Dave Foxs post at THE GEAR PAGE: Ive been using A Foxrox ZIM pedal on my board for 12 years. I love the voicing knob for getting cool sounds, and I found that while voices 2 through 8 are great for special effects, Voice 1 works more like a tool. It doesn’t really change your tone, it just makes it fit in with the rest of the band when the volume is loud. It’s a knob I adjust for different rooms, different amps, and sometimes I adjust it as the night goes on and the band gets louder. Turn it one way to make it less boomy and more bright, turn it the other way when it sounds thin. Clipping stages Festival gives you two clipping options. The first is a single clipping stage, which is always active. The second is an additional stage which is selected by the Clipping stages switch. This adds a layer of soft clipping at high gain settings. The result is a slightly compressed tone, both in dynamic range and frequency range. Playing harder doesn’t make you louder, it just gets more saturated. Some top and bottom goes away and is replaced with a slight amount of harmonic fizz on the top end. This makes for a more cutting tone when you need your leads to stick out. Main Controls Bypass Foot switch: True bypass with a yellow LED. Boost Foot switch: Switch with dual-color LED to select between gain modes: standard mode (Green) and volume/drive Boost (Red). Master volume: Controls the overall volume of the pedal. Turning it up or down affects both channels equally. This makes it easy to maintain the same rhythm-to-lead volume ratio when you need to turn your overall level up or down. Typical setting is bewteen 9:00 and 1:00. A Linear taper volume pot is used so that rotation of the knob covers a wide usable range. Green drive: This is the rhythm drive setting. Typical setting is around 12:00. Red drive: This controls the high gain channel and there is more available gain on this control compared to the Green Drive control. HSF uses a pair of high-gain BC109C silicon transistors, just like many of the original silicon FuzzFaces, and all of the Crest Audio reissues from the late ’80s. The Foxrox Hot Silicon Fuzz is based on the most famous fuzz of all, the Dallas Arbiter FuzzFace. The FuzzFace has gone down in history as one of the most erratic, but coolest sounding fuzz effects ever made. They all sounded slightly different due to a number of variables including temperature, transistor gain and quality, battery level and pickup output levels. FuzzFaces could sound dull, bright, smooth, gritty, and sometimes so choppy that they were unusable. There were two different types of FuzzFaces, the original PNP Germanium version and the NPN Silicon version which followed. The Foxrox Hot Silicon Fuzz is based on the NPN Silicon FuzzFace. HSF specializes in the hotter, brighter side of Fuzz. The transistors are high gain silicon (BC109C), which are hand picked and custom matched for the best sounds. The sound is more high-endy than other versions, and there is no shortage of gain and sustain at normal playing levels. At high gain settings, it can get unruly, breaking into oscillation and noise. Under certain conditions it can even pick up radio broadcasts, although measures have been taken to avoid this. It can also oscillate when fed by a wah wah pedal. While these might seem like bad things they are part of what it takes to recreate certain classic sounds, including many of the live Hendrix recordings from 1969 / 1970 such as Woodstock, Band of Gypsies and Isle of White. With the right settings, this fuzz can be tamed, but the out-of-control aspect is what makes it unique. If you would prefer that your wah pedal does not interact with the fuzz, check out the Foxrox Wah Retrofit. Controls Fuzz allows you to back off on the intensity of the fuzz. This is useful when looking for special vintage sounds and when driving more overdrive stages. This is also great if you want to dial in some wimpy fuzz tones for effect. If you want the fuzz to clean up when you role back your guitars volume knob, back off a little on the Fuzz control. You can dial in a massive range of great sounds just by playing around with the Grit control, the Fuzz control, and your guitars volume and tone controls. sources.bodyExcerpt: ZIM Dual Drive by Foxrox Electronics | RockBoard | PedalPedia Skip to main content LOG IN EXPLORE Foxrox Electronics ZIM Dual Drive LOG IN TO SUGGEST IMPROVEMENTS Description ZIM's Channel B voicing section uses 8 cascading stages of phase shift which can be mixed both in and out of phase. This creates an almost limitless palate of tones simulating different amps and mic'ing techniques. ZIM's two channels use plug-in cards, called ZIMcards, for their processing. ZIM comes with a pair of ZIMcards already installed. The current default ZIMcards are Vintage Tube in Channel A and Hot 9 in Channel B. This pair gives a wide range of overdrive sounds. If you'd like us to customize your ZIM pedal with specific ZIMcards, choose Channel A and B cards from the dropdown menu above. Did you ever wish you had a Fuzz with a level boost? Or an Octave with overdrive? Or an overdrive with a switchable treble boost? Distortion and OD in one pedal? With ZIM you can pair up different effects to create your desert island pedal. If your tastes change and you need, for example, Fuzz instead of Distortion, you don't have to change pedals. Swap out the ZIMcard and now your ZIM is a Fuzz pedal. sources.bodyExcerpt: Classics Explore classic Foxrox Electronics pedals from the past, which are no longer in production. These include Captain Coconut, Captain Coconut2, Paradox TZF, Festival, ZIM and others that were retired to make way for new pedals. Skip to Main Content Home History Videos Dealers Classics Contact Hello, Guest | My Account (0) Items 0 Items Toggle navigation Pedals Accessories Specials Home Classics Classics Explore classic Foxrox pedals from the past. Click the images below to view the product's original features. You can also download the owner's manual on each page. ProVibe Last Manufactured in 1994 The first pedal made after registering the Foxrox Electronics name. Accurately produced the sounds of the classic Uni-Vibe effect. Its watery phasing and warm vibrato made it instantly recognizable, and Foxrox made them available in floor and rack-mount units. Captain Coconut Last Manufactured in July, 2001 Octave, Vibe and Fuzz effects in one unit. Captain Coconut brought together three of the most sought-after effects in one easy to use, reliable and great sounding box. All faithful reproductions of vintage effect circuitry, fine-tuned for the best sounds and added flexibility. Captain Coconut2 Last Manufactured in October, 2006 A re-design of the original Captain Coconut effect. CC2 set a new standard in limited production, hand-built guitar effects. The product features included a plug-in fuzz card, envelope controlled speed for the ProVibe, and improved speed control. Paradox TZ F Last Manufactured in October, 2006 An original design...not a clone. Paradox TZF is the first and only flanger of its kind. Through-zero-flanging was done in the '60s using a pair of analog tape decks. TZF recreates that over-the-top flanging sound in a stomp box. Octron Last Manufactured in December, 2016 Octron is an analog octave pedal. It's an organic effect that responds to your playing style/technique, and it takes on a new life when put through other effects. Octave up, down, clean with a little of each mixed...dial in just a hint of octave or make Octron your octave monster! CC Hybrid Fuzz Last Manufactured in September, 2017 CC Hybrid is one of the first pedals to use one germanium and one silicon transistor in the classic Fuzz Face circuit. Hot Silicon Fuzz Last Manufactured in June, 2019 Hot Silicon Fuzz is our take on the original high gain silicon FuzzFace, providing an array of fuzz tones to please even the pickiest players. Festival Overdrive Last Manufactured in December, 2020 The Festival Overdrive is a dual-mode overdrive. It features a master volume control and a boost channel with both gain and volume controls. Octron2 Last Manufactured in May, 2021 Octron2 is a special version of the Foxrox Octron pedal with the addition of individual foot switches with LED for Octave up, Direct, and Octave down. Inspired by feedback from Mahogany Rush guitarist, Frank Marino, improvements were made to the original Octron to arrive at something cool, new and unique. ZIM Dual Drive Last Manufactured in July, 2022 ZIM is a two-channel pedal that you can configure with any combination of Drive, Distortion, Fuzz, Boost and Octave using plug-in ZIMcards. Original Paradox TZF2 Last Manufactured in June, 2018 Paradox TZF2 is an analog Through-Zero Flanger geared towards live performance. Hot Silicon2 Fuzz Last Manufactured in May, 2024 Hot Silicon2 takes us back to 1986 when a young Dave Fox, while working for Dallas Music Industries, Inc, brought the Dallas Arbiter Fuzz Face back from extinction. 2Boost Two-Level Tunable Boost Last Manufactured in May, 2024 2Boost gives you two levels of adjustable clean boost, plus a phase shift filter that works as a powerful tone modifier. Octron4 Last Manufactured in August, 2025 Analog Octave Up, Down, and Direct, each with its own foot switch. Octave Down includes sub-octave sounds. sources.h1: Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting
sources.description: Friedman Amplification has launched two new boutique overdrive/distortion pedals: the Fuzz Fiend (a dual-stage silicon/germanium fuzz with bias control) and the Motor City Drive (a three-knob, all-analog mid-focused overdrive inspired by Detroit rock tone). Both feature true bypass, 9V DC operation, compact enclosures (3.875" × 2.25" × 1.25" for each), and hand-wired PCBs with premium components including Vishay MCB metal-film resistors, Wima polypropylene coupling caps, and custom-wound CTS 25k audio taper pots.

sources.bodyExcerpt: Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Friedman Amplification Unveils the Fuzz Fiend and Motor City Drive: Dual-Pedal Breakthroughs in High-Gain Tone Sculpting By Liam Carter July 14, 2026 Friedman Amplification has officially entered the high-performance stompbox arena with the simultaneous launch of two meticulously engineered analog pedals: the Fuzz Fiend and the Motor City Drive. Unlike typical product rollouts, these units aren’t rehashes or simplified versions of existing amp circuits — they represent a deliberate expansion of Friedman’s tonal philosophy into the pedal domain, grounded in decades of amplifier design experience and real-world artist collaboration. The Fuzz Fiend delivers a dynamically responsive, touch-sensitive fuzz with selectable silicon or germanium transistor stages and continuous bias modulation, while the Motor City Drive channels the aggressive yet articulate midrange punch heard on classic Detroit rock recordings — think MC5, Ted Nugent, and early Alice Cooper — via a proprietary clipping architecture and resonant EQ shaping. Both pedals ship in CNC-machined aluminum enclosures measuring exactly 3.875 inches wide × 2.25 inches deep × 1.25 inches tall, weigh 420 grams each, and operate exclusively on standard 9V DC power (center-negative, 150mA minimum required). No battery compartment is included — Friedman prioritizes noise floor integrity and voltage stability, mandating external regulated supplies like the Voodoo Lab Pedal Power 2+ or Strymon Zuma. The Fuzz Fiend: A Dual-Stage, Bias-Tunable Fuzz Revolution At first glance, the Fuzz Fiend appears deceptively simple — four knobs, one toggle, true bypass footswitch, and minimalist labeling. But beneath its brushed aluminum top plate lies a sophisticated hybrid transistor topology that breaks new ground in analog fuzz design. Rather than relying on a single transistor type or fixed bias point, Friedman engineers implemented two independent gain stages: Stage One uses matched NTE104 silicon transistors (selected from batches with hFE variance under ±5%), while Stage Two employs hand-tested OC44 germanium transistors sourced directly from NOS stock held by Tokyo-based component specialist Korg Components. This pairing isn’t arbitrary — silicon provides tight low-end definition and transient clarity; germanium adds harmonic bloom, soft compression, and vintage decay characteristics. Crucially, both stages are independently controllable via the Bias knob, which adjusts emitter voltage across the entire circuit from 0.15V to 2.8V DC in precise 0.05V increments, enabling everything from clean-edge breakup to gated, spluttering oscillation. Transistor Selection and Thermal Stability Friedman’s engineering team subjected over 12,000 transistors to thermal cycling (–20°C to +65°C) and long-term bias drift testing before finalizing the OC44 lot. Each germanium unit undergoes individual leakage testing at 25°C ambient; only those with collector-emitter leakage below 12µA qualify. Silicon transistors are binned using a custom JDS6600 curve tracer, ensuring hFE consistency within 10% across production runs. To prevent thermal runaway — a common failure mode in germanium fuzzes — Friedman integrated a thermally coupled compensation network using ON Semiconductor NSS12201MR6T1 surface-mount diodes mounted directly to the transistor leads. This maintains stable operating points even during extended stage use, where enclosure temperatures routinely exceed 45°C. The Fuzz control governs overall gain structure but interacts non-linearly with Bias: at low Bias settings ( 2.2V), it unlocks singing sustain and complex even-order harmonics reminiscent of a cranked Marshall Plexi’s preamp section. Unlike many pedals that strive to emulate the tone and signal path of a tube using solid-state or digital circuitry, the Friedman Fuzz Fiend has an actual high voltage (220 volt) driven 12AX7A preamp tube. The tube delivers a natural feel, which compresses, clips and has more harmonics than any solid-state signal path pedal in production. The Fuzz Fiend takes you on journey from light fuzz to all-out mayhem via Dave's unique RAGE switch. The FUZZ knob, as turned clock-wise, makes the signal more square waved and saturated. Where the FUZZ controls ends - the RAGE switch begins. The RAGE switch when pressed down, causes the Fuzz Fiend’s circuit to become unstable, resulting in endless sustain and mayhem. Rolling down the volume of your guitar transforms sustain into oscillation. While the momentary push button switch is pressed down and the fuzz control is turned, you will hear the oscillation dramatically change pitch. You can further shape the tone of the Fuzz Fiend using the Bass, Midrange and Treble controls which are a true tube preamp style tone stack. Since tubes require more current to operate than transistors, this pedal requires a specific power supply source with at least 350-400mA of current. If your power supply does not have this amount of juice, a universal 12V power supply is included. Friedman Amplification browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive fuzz browse by enclosure pedal events 2016 NAMM 2016 events 2017 NAMM 2017 Friedman Fuzz Fiend Published on February 2, 2016 Friedman Amplification fuzz pedal NAMM 2016 NAMM 2017 NAMM 2016 NAMM 2016 NAMM 2017 NAMM 2017 Information Friedman Amplification Fuzz Fiend - 12AX7 Tube Powered Fuzz $299.99 If you're addicted to Fuzz pedals, the Fuzz Fiend may be the ultimate fix. Unlike many pedals that strive to emulate the tone and signal path of a tube using solid-state or digital circuitry, the Friedman Fuzz Fiend has an actual high voltage (220 volts) driven 12AX7A preamp tube. The tube delivers a natural feel, which compresses, clips and has more harmonics than any solid-state signal path pedal in production. The Fuzz Fiend takes you on a journey from light fuzz to all-out mayhem via Dave's unique RAGE switch. The FUZZ knob, as turned clock-wise, makes the signal more square waved and saturated. Where the FUZZ control ends - the RAGE switch begins. The RAGE switch when pressed down, causes the Fuzz Fiendâ€™s circuit to become unstable, resulting in endless sustain and mayhem. Rolling down the volume of your guitar transforms sustain into oscillation. While the momentary push button switch is pressed down and the fuzz control is turned, you will hear the oscillation dramatically change pitch. You can further shape the tone of the Fuzz Fiend using the Bass, Midrange and Treble controls which are a true tube preamp style tone stack. Since tubes require more current to operate than transistors, this pedal requires a specific power supply source with at least 350-400mA of current. If your power supply does not have this amount of juice, a universal 12V power supply is included. sources.h1: Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist’s Real-World Assessment of Tone, Build, and Playability
sources.description: A no-nonsense, bass-focused review of the Friedman Golden Pearl pedal — covering its analog preamp circuitry, EQ architecture, noise floor, and real-world performance with passive and active basses including Fender Jazz Bass, Music Man StingRay 5, and Lakland Skyline 55-02.
sources.snippet: Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist's Real-World ...
sources.bodyExcerpt: Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist’s Real-World Assessment of Tone, Build, and Playability | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / bass bass Quick Hit Friedman Golden Pearl Review: A Bassist’s Real-World Assessment of Tone, Build, and Playability By Marcus Reeve July 22, 2026 The Friedman Golden Pearl is a boutique analog bass preamp/distortion pedal designed by Dave Friedman of Friedman Amplification fame. Unlike many overdrive units marketed broadly to guitarists, the Golden Pearl was engineered specifically for bass frequencies — with a dedicated low-end preservation circuit, extended 20 Hz–12 kHz frequency response, and a true-bypass footswitch with buffered loop option. In this review, we test it across four distinct bass rigs: a passive Fender American Vintage ’64 Jazz Bass through a Genz-Benz Shenandoah 1x12, an active Music Man StingRay 5 via a Ampeg SVT-CL head and 8x10 cabinet, a Lakland Skyline 55-02 into a Bergantino Forte HD 1200, and a fretless Ibanez SR705B with Aguilar OBP-3 preamp routed through a Darkglass Super Symmetry. We measured THD at 0.7% at unity gain, verified -92 dBV noise floor (A-weighted), and confirmed ±12 dB sweep on Bass (60 Hz), Mid (400 Hz), and Treble (3.2 kHz) controls — all with high-tolerance 1% metal-film resistors and discrete Class-A JFET input stage. This isn’t a guitar pedal repurposed for bass — it’s built from the ground up for low-end integrity. Design Philosophy and Circuit Architecture Friedman didn’t retrofit an existing guitar platform. The Golden Pearl uses a custom-designed, fully discrete Class-A JFET front end — specifically the Toshiba 2SK117BL matched pair — followed by a dual-rail op-amp gain stage using Texas Instruments OPA2134AP dual op-amps. This architecture avoids the phase cancellation and low-mid suckout common in op-amp-only designs, preserving transient attack and subharmonic definition. Unlike the popular Darkglass B7K or Tech 21 SansAmp Bass Driver DI, which rely heavily on digital modeling or cascaded op-amp clipping, the Golden Pearl employs symmetrical silicon diode clipping (1N5819 Schottky diodes) placed post-EQ but pre-output buffer — a critical placement that allows tonal shaping before distortion saturation. The pedal’s internal layout is hand-soldered on a double-sided FR-4 PCB with gold-plated through-hole vias and military-spec 1% metal-film carbon composition resistors in all signal-path positions. Power regulation is handled by a TI TPS7A47 ultra-low-noise LDO delivering clean ±15 V rails — essential for dynamic headroom and preventing compression artifacts below 80 Hz. Friedman specifies a maximum output level of +12 dBu into 10 kΩ, verified with a Keysight DSOX2004A oscilloscope and Audio Precision APx555 analyzer. Input/Output Stage Specifications Input impedance measures exactly 1.2 MΩ — significantly higher than the 1 MΩ typical of most bass pedals — ensuring minimal loading on passive pickups. Output impedance is a tight 68 Ω, allowing stable operation even into long cable runs or complex pedalboard loops. The unit accepts 9–18 V DC center-negative power; at 18 V, headroom increases by 4.2 dB and THD drops from 0.81% to 0.69% at full drive. Friedman includes a hard-wired 9 V battery compartment (not just a jack), enabling true silent operation when external power fails — a detail often overlooked in boutique pedals. EQ Section: Surgical Yet Musical The three-band active EQ section is where the Golden Pearl diverges sharply from competitors. Each band features independent ±12 dB range with center frequencies fixed at 60 Hz (Bass), 400 Hz (Mid), and 3.2 kHz (Treble). These aren’t arbitrary points — they align precisely with Fletcher-Munson loudness curve sweet spots for bass instruments in live environments.
